questions.sub_topic: Derivation of Molar Mass from RLVP
questions.question: For a very dilute solution containing \( w_2 \) grams of non-volatile solute (molar mass \( M_2 \)) in \( w_1 \) grams of solvent (molar mass \( M_1 \)), Raoult's law gives:
options: A) \( \frac{P^\circ - P}{P^\circ} = \frac{w_2 \cdot M_1}{M_2 \cdot w_1} \)
B) \( \frac{P^\circ - P}{P^\circ} = \frac{w_2 \cdot w_1}{M_2 \cdot M_1} \)
C) \( \frac{P^\circ - P}{P^\circ} = \frac{M_2 \cdot w_1}{w_2 \cdot M_1} \)
D) \( \frac{P^\circ - P}{P^\circ} = \frac{w_2 \cdot M_2}{w_1 \cdot M_1} \)
questions.explanation: \( \frac{P^\circ - P}{P^\circ} = \chi_2 = \frac{n_2}{n_1 + n_2} \approx \frac{n_2}{n_1} = \frac{w_2/M_2}{w_1/M_1} = \frac{w_2 \cdot M_1}{M_2 \cdot w_1} \).

questions.question: What is the boiling point of an aqueous solution containing 0.1 mol of glucose and 0.1 mol of urea dissolved together in 1000 g of water? (\( K_b \) of water = 0.52 K kg/mol)
questions.explanation: Both are non-electrolytes. Total molality of solute particles \( m_{\text{total}} = 0.1 + 0.1 = 0.2\text{ mol/kg} \). Elevation \( \Delta T_b = K_b m_{\text{total}} = 0.52 \times 0.2 = 0.104\text{ K} \). Boiling point = \( 100 + 0.104 = 100.104^\circ\text{C} \).

questions.question: A substance A trimerizes in solution according to \( 3\ce{A <=> A3} \) with degree of association \( \alpha = 0.90 \). The Van't Hoff factor (\( i \)) of the solute is:
In commercial reverse osmosis desalination, thin-film composite membranes made of cellulose acetate or polyamide are permeable to water but impermeable to sodium and chloride ions because:
options: A) High hydration energy creates large hydrated ionic shells that are excluded by size and electrostatic charge from the membrane pores
B) Cellulose acetate chemically dissolves sodium metal into gas
C) Chloride ions are converted to insoluble chlorine polymers
D) The membrane creates a permanent zero-gravity field
questions.explanation: Water molecules pass through microscopic sub-nanometer pores, while strongly hydrated \( \ce{Na^+} \) and \( \ce{Cl^-} \) ions have large effective radii and dielectric exclusion, preventing passage.

questions.question: Azeotropic mixtures can be separated into pure components by 'pressure-swing distillation' because:
options: A) The azeotropic composition changes with changing external pressure
B) Azeotropes boil at absolute zero at elevated pressure
C) High pressure converts ideal solutions into pure elements
D) One component freezes into a solid at any applied pressure
questions.explanation: Because the vapour pressure curves of the two components vary differently with temperature, changing system pressure shifts or eliminates the azeotropic composition, enabling complete separation across two columns.

questions.question: In the Apollo space missions, the hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell was chosen to supply electrical power primarily because:
options: A) It produces radioactive shielding around the spacecraft
B) It operates without consuming any hydrogen gas
C) It generates electricity with high efficiency and the reaction product (pure water) served as drinking water for astronauts
D) It creates artificial gravity inside the cockpit
questions.explanation: The \( \ce{H2-O2} \) fuel cell provided reliable power with high energy density and produced pure potable water used directly by the astronauts.

questions.question: In the impressed current method of cathodic protection for underground pipelines:
options: A) The pipeline is connected to the positive terminal of an AC generator
B) The iron metal is converted entirely into liquid mercury
C) The soil is neutralized with concentrated hydrochloric acid
D) An external direct current source forces electrons into the pipeline, making it an unreactive cathode
questions.explanation: An external DC power supply connects the iron pipe to the negative terminal (making it the cathode where reduction occurs), while an inert scrap anode corrodes in its place.

questions.question: Given \( \lambda_m^\circ(\ce{Mg^{2+}}) = 106.0\text{ S}\cdot\text{cm}^2/\text{mol} \) and \( \lambda_m^\circ(\ce{SO4^{2-}}) = 160.0\text{ S}\cdot\text{cm}^2/\text{mol} \). What is the limiting equivalent conductivity (\( \Lambda_{eq}^\circ \)) of \( \ce{MgSO4} \)?
options: A) \( 266.0\text{ S}\cdot\text{cm}^2/\text{eq} \)
B) \( 133.0\text{ S}\cdot\text{cm}^2/\text{eq} \)
C) \( 53.0\text{ S}\cdot\text{cm}^2/\text{eq} \)
D) \( 66.5\text{ S}\cdot\text{cm}^2/\text{eq} \)
questions.explanation: \( \Lambda_m^\circ(\ce{MgSO4}) = 106.0 + 160.0 = 266.0\text{ S}\cdot\text{cm}^2/\text{mol} \). For \( \ce{MgSO4} \), \( n = 2 \). Equivalent conductivity \( \Lambda_{eq}^\circ = \Lambda_m^\circ / n = 266.0 / 2 = 133.0\text{ S}\cdot\text{cm}^2/\text{eq} \).

questions.question: For the half-reaction \( \ce{Cr2O7^{2-} + 14H^+ + 6e^- -> 2Cr^{3+} + 7H2O} \) at 298 K, increasing the pH of the solution by 1 unit causes the reduction potential to:
options: A) Increase by 0.059 V
B) Decrease by 0.059 V
C) Remain completely unchanged
D) Decrease by \( \frac{14 \times 0.059}{6} \approx 0.138\text{ V} \)
questions.explanation: \( E = E^\circ - \frac{0.059}{6} \log \frac{[\ce{Cr^{3+}}]^2}{[\ce{Cr2O7^{2-}}][\ce{H^+}]^{14}} = E' - \frac{14 \times 0.059}{6} \text{pH} \). Increasing pH by 1 decreases potential by \( 14 \times 0.059 / 6 \approx 0.138\text{ V} \).

questions.sub_topic: Temperature Coefficient and Entropy of Cell
questions.question: The temperature coefficient of electromotive force of a reversible cell is \( \left(\frac{\partial E}{\partial T}\right)_P \). The entropy change (\( \Delta S \)) of the cell reaction is related to this coefficient by:
options: A) \( \Delta S = n F \left(\frac{\partial E}{\partial T}\right)_P \)
B) \( \Delta S = -n F \left(\frac{\partial E}{\partial T}\right)_P \)
C) \( \Delta S = \frac{n F}{T} \left(\frac{\partial E}{\partial T}\right)_P \)
D) \( \Delta S = n F E \cdot T \)
questions.explanation: From thermodynamics: \( \left(\frac{\partial \Delta G}{\partial T}\right)_P = -\Delta S \). Since \( \Delta G = -nFE \), differentiating with respect to \( T \) gives \( -nF \left(\frac{\partial E}{\partial T}\right)_P = -\Delta S \implies \Delta S = nF \left(\frac{\partial E}{\partial T}\right)_P \).

questions.question: For a general \( n \)-th order chemical reaction (where \( n \neq 1 \)), the half-life period \( t_{1/2} \) is proportional to:
questions.explanation: Integrated rate law for \( n \)-th order gives \( t_{1/2} = \frac{2^{n-1}-1}{k(n-1)[A]_0^{n-1}} \propto [A]_0^{1-n} \).

questions.question: The steady-state approximation applied to a reactive intermediate (I) in a reaction mechanism assumes that:
options: A) The intermediate never reacts to form products
B) The concentration of intermediate equals the concentration of reactant
C) The net rate of change of concentration of the intermediate is approximately zero (\( d[I]/dt \approx 0 \))
D) The reaction rate is independent of temperature
questions.explanation: Because a reactive intermediate is formed and consumed rapidly, its concentration remains very small and virtually constant, allowing \( d[I]/dt \approx 0 \).

questions.question: In chemical kinetics, threshold energy (\( E_{\text{threshold}} \)) of a reaction is defined as the:
options: A) Energy difference between products and reactants (\( \Delta H \))
B) Energy released when the activated complex decomposes
C) Zero point vibrational energy of the solvent
D) Minimum energy that colliding molecules must possess to react, equal to (Initial average energy + Activation energy)
questions.explanation: \( E_{\text{threshold}} = E_{\text{average}} + E_a \). It is the total energy barrier that colliding reactant molecules must attain to form the activated complex.

questions.question: In a reaction coordinate potential energy profile, how does a transition state differ fundamentally from an intermediate?
options: A) A transition state corresponds to an energy maximum with partially formed bonds and cannot be isolated, while an intermediate is a local energy minimum with real chemical bonds
B) A transition state is a stable chemical substance with long lifetime
C) An intermediate lies at the highest energy peak of the profile
D) A transition state has zero potential energy
questions.explanation: A transition state represents an activated complex at the peak of an energy barrier (lifetime ~\( 10^{-13}\text{ s} \)), whereas an intermediate sits in a shallow potential energy valley.

questions.question: According to the Michaelis-Menten enzyme rate equation \( v = \frac{V_{\text{max}}[S]}{K_m + [S]} \), at very high substrate concentrations (\( [S] \gg K_m \)), the reaction follows:
options: A) First-order kinetics with rate proportional to \( [S] \)
B) Zero-order kinetics with rate equal to \( V_{\text{max}} \)
C) Second-order kinetics
D) Fractional order 0.5
questions.explanation: When \( [S] \gg K_m \), the denominator \( K_m + [S] \approx [S] \), simplifying the equation to \( v = V_{\text{max}} \). All active sites on the enzyme are saturated, so rate is zero order in substrate.

questions.topic: Unit IV: d and f Block Elements
questions.sub_topic: Electronic Configuration of Europium and Terbium
questions.question: Europium (\( Z = 63 \)) and Terbium (\( Z = 65 \)) have electronic configurations of \( [\ce{Xe}]\,4f^7\,6s^2 \) and \( [\ce{Xe}]\,4f^9\,6s^2 \). Europium exhibits a stable +2 oxidation state because \( \ce{Eu^{2+}} \) has:
options: A) A completely filled \( 4f^{14} \) configuration
B) A stable half-filled \( 4f^7 \) configuration
C) Zero 4f electrons
D) An empty 5d subshell
questions.explanation: Loss of two 6s electrons leaves \( \ce{Eu^{2+}} \) with the half-filled, spherically symmetrical \( 4f^7 \) subshell, which has extra stability.

questions.topic: Unit IV: d and f Block Elements
questions.question: What are the geometries of chromate ion (\( \ce{CrO4^{2-}} \)) and dichromate ion (\( \ce{Cr2O7^{2-}} \))?
options: A) Both are planar square complexes
B) Chromate is octahedral; dichromate is linear
C) Both are trigonal bipyramidal
D) Chromate is tetrahedral; dichromate consists of two sharing tetrahedra with a bridging Cr-O-Cr bond angle of ~126°
questions.explanation: Chromate is a discrete tetrahedral ion. Dichromate consists of two corner-sharing \( \ce{CrO4} \) tetrahedra linked through a common bridging oxygen atom with a \( \ce{Cr-O-Cr} \) angle of 126°.

questions.topic: Unit IV: d and f Block Elements
questions.question: The steady decrease in ionic radii across the actinoid series (actinoid contraction) is more pronounced than lanthanoid contraction because:
options: A) Actinoids have lower atomic numbers than lanthanoids
B) 5f electrons have a more diffuse spatial distribution and shield nuclear charge less effectively than 4f electrons
C) 4f electrons have zero angular momentum
D) Actinoids do not contain valence d-orbitals
questions.explanation: 5f orbitals are more radially extended and diffuse than 4f orbitals, providing weaker shielding per electron. Consequently, the effective nuclear charge increases more rapidly across actinoids.

questions.topic: Unit IV: d and f Block Elements
questions.sub_topic: Highest Oxidation States: OsO4 and RuO4
questions.question: Which transition metal group elements form tetroxides (\( \ce{MO4} \)) exhibiting the highest oxidation state (+8) in transition metal chemistry?
options: A) Iron (Fe) and Cobalt (Co)
B) Ruthenium (Ru) and Osmium (Os)
C) Chromium (Cr) and Molybdenum (Mo)
D) Manganese (Mn) and Rhenium (Re)
questions.explanation: In Group 8, heavier congeners Ruthenium and Osmium can engage all 8 valence electrons (\( d^6 s^2 \)) in bonding with oxygen, forming volatile tetroxides \( \ce{RuO4} \) and \( \ce{OsO4} \) in the +8 oxidation state.

questions.topic: Unit IV: d and f Block Elements
questions.question: Ziegler-Natta catalyst used for the stereospecific coordination polymerization of ethene into high-density polyethene (HDPE) chemically consists of:
options: A) Vanadium pentoxide (\( \ce{V2O5} \)) and platinum black
B) Nickel carbonyl (\( \ce{Ni(CO)4} \)) and dry ether
C) Copper sulphate and sodium borohydride
D) Titanium tetrachloride (\( \ce{TiCl4} \)) and triethylaluminium (\( \ce{Al(C2H5)3} \))
questions.explanation: The heterogeneous Ziegler-Natta catalyst combination \( \ce{TiCl4 + Al(C2H5)3} \) coordinates alkene monomers at vacant titanium coordination sites to synthesize linear HDPE under low pressure.

questions.question: According to the 18-electron rule, what is the value of \( x \) in the mononuclear binary carbonyl \( [\ce{Cr(CO)}_x] \)?
questions.explanation: Chromium (Cr) has 6 valence electrons (\( 3d^5 4s^1 \)). Each CO ligand donates 2 electrons. For 18 valence electrons: \( 6 + 2x = 18 \implies 2x = 12 \implies x = 6 \). Complex is \( [\ce{Cr(CO)6}] \).

questions.question: For the octahedral complex \( [\ce{Co(en)2Cl2}]^+ \):
options: A) The trans isomer is chiral and optically active
B) The cis isomer is chiral and optically active (existing as a pair of enantiomers), while the trans isomer is achiral and optically inactive
C) Both cis and trans isomers are optically active
D) Neither isomer exhibits optical activity
questions.explanation: The trans isomer has an inversion center and a plane of symmetry (achiral). The cis isomer lacks any improper axis of rotation (chiral \( C_2 \) symmetry) and exists as dextro and laevo enantiomers.

questions.sub_topic: CFSE for Low-Spin d5 Octahedral Complexes
questions.question: Calculate the Crystal Field Stabilization Energy (CFSE) of a low-spin octahedral \( d^5 \) complex (such as \( [\ce{Fe(CN)6}]^{3-} \)):
options: B) \( -1.2 \Delta_o + P \)
questions.explanation: In low spin \( d^5 \), all 5 electrons pair in \( t_{2g} \): \( t_{2g}^5\,e_g^0 \). \( \text{CFSE} = 5(-0.4\Delta_o) = -2.0\Delta_o \). Two electron pairs are forced beyond the free ion ground state, giving pairing energy \( +2P \).

questions.question: The complex \( [\ce{Fe(CN)6}]^{3-} \) has an enormous formation constant (\( K_f \approx 10^{31} \)), yet when mixed with radio-labeled \( \ce{^{14}CN^-} \), exchange is virtually undetectable over days. This complex is:
options: A) Thermodynamically unstable and kinetically labile
B) Thermodynamically stable but kinetically labile
C) Thermodynamically unstable and kinetically inert
D) Thermodynamically highly stable and kinetically inert
questions.explanation: A high formation constant reflects thermodynamic stability. The absence of ligand substitution signifies a high activation energy barrier for substitution, denoting kinetic inertness.

questions.question: In the synergic bonding of transition metal carbonyls, back-donation occurs from:
options: A) Filled \( \pi \) bonding orbitals of CO into empty metal s-orbitals
B) Filled metal d-orbitals into empty \( \pi^* \) antibonding orbitals of the carbon monoxide ligand
C) Empty metal d-orbitals into filled \( \sigma \) orbitals of CO
D) Outer sphere counter ions into the metal nucleus
questions.explanation: The synergic bonding consists of a \( \sigma \) bond (CO lone pair \( \to \) vacant metal d) and a \( \pi \) back-bond (filled metal \( d_{xy}/d_{yz}/d_{zx} \to \) vacant \( \pi^* \) of CO).

questions.question: What is the correct decreasing order of reactivity towards solvolysis (\( \text{S}_{\text{N}}1 \)) among the following halides?
options: A) Benzyl chloride > Allyl chloride > Isopropyl chloride > Vinyl chloride
B) Vinyl chloride > Isopropyl chloride > Allyl chloride > Benzyl chloride
C) Allyl chloride > Vinyl chloride > Benzyl chloride > Isopropyl chloride
D) Isopropyl chloride > Benzyl chloride > Allyl chloride > Vinyl chloride
questions.explanation: Benzyl and allyl carbocations are resonance-stabilized. Isopropyl carbocation is secondary. Vinyl cation is extremely unstable and vinyl chloride has partial double-bond character.

questions.sub_topic: Benzyne Mechanism in Nucleophilic Aromatic Substitution
questions.question: When chlorobenzene labeled with \( \ce{^{14}C} \) at C1 is treated with potassium amide (\( \ce{KNH2} \)) in liquid ammonia, aniline is formed with the amino group attached 50% to C1 and 50% to C2. This proves the reaction proceeds via an:
options: A) Addition-elimination Meisenheimer pathway
B) Elimination-addition mechanism involving a neutral Benzyne intermediate
C) \( \text{S}_{\text{N}}2 \) backside attack mechanism
D) Electrophilic aromatic substitution mechanism
questions.explanation: Strong base \( \ce{NH2^-} \) abstracts an ortho proton, eliminating chloride to form a transient benzyne (dehydrobenzene) intermediate with a formal triple bond, which is attacked with equal probability at C1 and C2.

questions.question: The specific rotation \( [\alpha]_D^T \) of an optically active liquid in a polarimeter tube of length \( l \) decimeters and concentration \( c \) g/mL is calculated using:
options: A) \( [\alpha]_D^T = \frac{\alpha}{l \times c} \)
B) \( [\alpha]_D^T = \frac{\alpha \times l}{c} \)
C) \( [\alpha]_D^T = \frac{l \times c}{\alpha} \)
D) \( [\alpha]_D^T = \alpha \times l \times c \)
questions.explanation: Specific optical rotation is normalized for path length and concentration: \( [\alpha] = \frac{\alpha}{l \cdot c} \), where \( \alpha \) is observed rotation in degrees, \( l \) is in dm, and \( c \) is in g/mL.

questions.question: Iodoform (\( \ce{CHI3} \)) was historically widely used as an antiseptic dressing for wounds. Its therapeutic antiseptic property is due to:
options: A) The specific action of the central carbon-hydrogen bond
B) Its complete insolubility in water
C) The slow liberation of free elemental iodine when it comes in contact with tissue fluids
D) Its sweet chloroform-like odor
questions.explanation: Iodoform itself is not an active antiseptic; in contact with living tissue fluids, it slowly decomposes to liberate elemental iodine (\( \ce{I2} \)), which acts as the active germicidal agent.

questions.question: Heating 2-bromonitrobenzene with copper powder yields 2,2'-dinitrobiphenyl in high yield via the Ullmann reaction. Why do ortho-nitro groups accelerate the Ullmann coupling?
options: A) The electron-withdrawing nitro group stabilizes the intermediate organocopper species
B) The nitro group donates electrons to decompose the copper powder
C) The nitro group hydrolyzes the bromine atom to water
D) The reaction becomes explosive at room temperature
questions.explanation: Electron-withdrawing substituents (especially ortho to the halogen) facilitate oxidative addition of copper into the aryl-halogen bond and stabilize the resulting arylcopper intermediate.

questions.topic: Unit VII: Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
questions.question: Arrange the following compounds in order of INCREASING acid strength: (I) Phenol, (II) p-Cresol, (III) p-Nitrophenol, (IV) Ethanol:
options: A) \( \text{IV} < \text{I} < \text{II} < \text{III} \)
B) \( \text{IV} < \text{II} < \text{I} < \text{III} \)
C) \( \text{I} < \text{II} < \text{III} < \text{IV} \)
D) \( \text{III} < \text{I} < \text{II} < \text{IV} \)
questions.explanation: Ethanol is least acidic (aliphatic). p-Cresol is less acidic than phenol due to electron-donating methyl group (+I, hyperconjugation). p-Nitrophenol is most acidic due to \( -I \) and \( -M \) effects of nitro group. Hence \( \text{IV} < \text{II} < \text{I} < \text{III} \).

questions.topic: Unit VII: Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
questions.question: When vapours of tert-butyl alcohol (2-methylpropan-2-ol) are passed over heated copper at 573 K, what reaction occurs?
options: A) Dehydrogenation to 2-methylpropanal
B) Oxidation to acetone and carbon dioxide
C) Dehydration to 2-methylpropene (isobutylene)
D) No reaction takes place
questions.explanation: Tertiary alcohols have no \( \alpha \)-hydrogen atom on the carbinol carbon and cannot undergo dehydrogenation. Instead, over hot copper at 573 K they undergo dehydration to alkenes (isobutylene).

questions.topic: Unit VII: Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
questions.sub_topic: Claisen Rearrangement of Allyl Aryl Ethers
questions.question: Thermal rearrangement of allyl phenyl ether at 473 K yields ortho-allylphenol via:
options: A) A free radical chain cleavage mechanism
B) An intermolecular electrophilic addition
C) A concerted [3,3]-sigmatropic rearrangement (Claisen rearrangement)
D) An elimination-addition benzyne pathway
questions.explanation: Allyl aryl ethers undergo concerted intramolecular [3,3]-sigmatropic shift through a 6-membered cyclic chair transition state with complete inversion of the allyl chain to give 2-allylphenol.

questions.topic: Unit VII: Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
questions.question: In the acid-catalyzed rearrangement of cumene hydroperoxide to phenol and acetone, the migratory group that shifts from carbon to electron-deficient oxygen is the:
options: A) Methyl group
B) Hydride ion
C) Hydroxyl group
D) Phenyl group
questions.explanation: Protonation and loss of water from the hydroperoxide generates an electron-deficient oxygen. The phenyl group has higher migratory aptitude than methyl and migrates with its electron pair to oxygen.

questions.topic: Unit VII: Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
questions.question: The cyclic polyether 18-crown-6 selectively binds which alkali metal cation because its ionic cavity size (~2.7 Å) matches the cation diameter?
options: A) Lithium ion (\( \ce{Li^+} \))
B) Sodium ion (\( \ce{Na^+} \))
C) Potassium ion (\( \ce{K^+} \))
D) Cesium ion (\( \ce{Cs^+} \))
questions.explanation: 18-crown-6 has a cavity size of 2.6-3.2 Å that perfectly complements the ionic diameter of \( \ce{K^+} \) (2.66 Å). (12-crown-4 binds \( \ce{Li^+} \); 15-crown-5 binds \( \ce{Na^+} \)).

questions.topic: Unit VIII: Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: In a positive Tollens' test for aldehydes, what is the change in oxidation state of silver?
options: A) From 0 to +1
B) From +2 to +1
C) From +1 to +2
D) From +1 in \( [\ce{Ag(NH3)2}]^+ \) to 0 in metallic \( \ce{Ag} \)
questions.explanation: \( \ce{RCHO + 2[Ag(NH3)2]^+ + 3OH^- -> RCOO^- + 2Ag(s) + 4NH3 + 2H2O} \). Silver is reduced from +1 to elemental silver (0), forming a mirror.

questions.topic: Unit VIII: Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: When benzaldehyde is subjected to the Cannizzaro reaction in heavy water (\( \ce{D2O} \)) with \( \ce{NaOD} \), the benzyl alcohol formed contains:
options: A) Two deuterium atoms on the benzylic carbon (\( \ce{C6H5CD2OD} \))
B) One deuterium on the benzylic carbon (\( \ce{C6H5CHDOD} \))
C) No deuterium attached to the benzylic carbon (\( \ce{C6H5CH2OD} \)), proving that hydride is transferred directly between two aldehyde molecules
D) Deuterium on all aromatic ring carbons
questions.explanation: The hydride ion is transferred directly from one benzaldehyde molecule to the other without ever coming into contact with solvent water, so no D is incorporated at the benzylic carbon.

questions.topic: Unit VIII: Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: In the HVZ reaction, the carboxylic acid is first converted into an acid halide by phosphorus trihalide because:
options: A) Carboxylic acids cannot dissolve phosphorus
B) Acid halides enolize much more readily than free carboxylic acids
C) Free carboxylic acids decompose into carbon monoxide with halogens
D) Acid halides have higher boiling points than carboxylic acids
questions.explanation: Free carboxylic acids undergo enolization very poorly due to resonance stabilization of the carboxyl group. Acyl halides enolize readily, presenting a nucleophilic \( \alpha \)-carbon that attacks molecular halogen.

questions.topic: Unit VIII: Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: What is the correct decreasing order of reactivity of carboxylic acid derivatives towards nucleophilic acyl substitution?
options: A) Amide > Ester > Acid anhydride > Acyl chloride
B) Ester > Acyl chloride > Acid anhydride > Amide
C) Acyl chloride > Acid anhydride > Ester > Amide
D) Acid anhydride > Acyl chloride > Amide > Ester
questions.explanation: Reactivity depends on leaving group ability (\( \ce{Cl^- > RCOO^- > RO^- > NH2^-} \)) and resonance stabilization of the carbonyl carbon by the heteroatom.

questions.topic: Unit VIII: Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids
questions.question: Heating gem-dicarboxylic acids like malonic acid results in decarboxylation through a concerted 6-membered cyclic transition state yielding initially:
options: A) The enol form of acetic acid, which rapidly tautomerizes to acetic acid
B) A high-energy carbene intermediate
C) A free acetate radical in solvent cage
D) Carbon monoxide and formaldehyde
questions.explanation: The cyclic mechanism transfers the acidic hydrogen to the adjacent carbonyl oxygen while expelling \( \ce{CO2} \), producing enol \( \ce{CH2=C(OH)2} \), which tautomerizes to stable acetic acid.

questions.question: In the Gabriel phthalimide synthesis, potassium phthalimide reacts with an alkyl halide via which mechanism?
options: A) \( \text{S}_{\text{N}}1 \) carbocation substitution
B) E2 elimination
C) Electrophilic aromatic substitution
D) \( \text{S}_{\text{N}}2 \) nucleophilic substitution
questions.explanation: The phthalimide anion acts as a nucleophile, displacing the halide from primary alkyl halides in a bimolecular \( \text{S}_{\text{N}}2 \) displacement.

questions.question: Why do secondary and tertiary amines fail to give the carbylamine test?
options: A) Secondary and tertiary amines are completely insoluble in alcohol
B) They oxidize potassium hydroxide to potassium peroxide
C) The formation of an isocyanide (\( \ce{R-N#C} \)) requires two replaceable hydrogen atoms on the nitrogen atom
D) They do not react with chloroform under any conditions
questions.explanation: The mechanism involves initial attack of amine on dichlorocarbene followed by two successive base-induced eliminations of \( \ce{HCl} \). This requires two protons on nitrogen, which only primary amines have.

questions.question: To prepare 4-bromoaniline from aniline without forming 2,4,6-tribromoaniline, the strategy employed is:
options: A) Bromination at 500 K in gaseous state
B) Direct bromination in the presence of metallic sodium
C) Reaction with \( \ce{HBr} \) in dark
D) Acetylation with \( \ce{(CH3CO)2O} \) to acetanilide, bromination with \( \ce{Br2/CH3COOH} \), and alkaline hydrolysis
questions.explanation: Acetanilide moderates nitrogen electron donation via resonance with the acetyl carbonyl. Bromination then cleanly gives 4-bromoacetanilide, which on hydrolysis yields 4-bromoaniline.

questions.sub_topic: Zwitterion Dipolar Properties of Sulphanilic Acid
questions.question: Sulphanilic acid has a very high decomposition temperature (>553 K) and is insoluble in organic solvents like ether and benzene because:
options: A) It forms a giant 3D covalent diamond lattice
B) It exists as a dipolar zwitterion having strong electrostatic ionic lattice forces
C) It undergoes spontaneous polymerization into nylon
D) It is completely non-polar and hydrophobic
questions.explanation: Sulphanilic acid exists as internal dipolar salt \( \ce{^+H3N-C6H4-SO3^-} \). Strong ionic attractions in the crystal lattice require high thermal energy to disrupt, imparting salt-like physical properties.

questions.question: Azo coupling of benzenediazonium chloride with phenol is optimal at pH 9-10, whereas coupling with aniline is optimal at pH 4-5. Why?
options: A) At pH 9-10, phenol is converted to the more reactive phenoxide nucleophile; at pH 4-5, aniline is unprotonated while diazonium cation remains stable
B) At pH 9-10, diazonium ion becomes a stronger electrophile
C) Phenol is destroyed below pH 7
D) Aniline only dissolves in strongly alkaline solutions
questions.explanation: Phenoxide ion (\( \ce{C6H5O^-} \)) is far more reactive than neutral phenol towards electrophilic coupling. For aniline, basic pH converts diazonium to unreactive diazohydroxide, while acidic pH (<4) protonates aniline to unreactive anilinium.

questions.question: When pure \( \alpha \)-D-glucose (+112°) or pure \( \beta \)-D-glucose (+19°) is dissolved in water, the specific rotation gradually changes until reaching an equilibrium value of +52.7°. At equilibrium, the percentage composition is approximately:
options: A) 50% \( \alpha \)-D-glucose and 50% \( \beta \)-D-glucose
B) 80% \( \alpha \)-D-glucose and 20% \( \beta \)-D-glucose
C) 36% \( \alpha \)-D-glucose, 64% \( \beta \)-D-glucose, and <0.02% open-chain form
D) 100% open-chain aldehyde form
questions.explanation: \( \beta \)-D-glucopyranose is more stable (64%) because all bulky substituents (-OH and -CH2OH) occupy equatorial positions in its chair conformation.

questions.question: The peptide linkage (-CO-NH-) in proteins is strictly planar and rigid with restricted rotation because:
options: A) Carbon and nitrogen are linked by a triple bond
B) Resonance delocalizes the nitrogen lone pair, imparting ~40% double-bond character to the C-N bond
C) Hydrogen bonding prevents all vibrational motion
D) Steric hindrance from side chains prevents bond rotation
questions.explanation: Resonance \( \ce{-C(=O)-NH- <=> -C(O^-)=N^+H-} \) gives the C-N bond partial double bond character (length 1.32 Å vs normal 1.47 Å), restricting rotation and keeping the 6 atoms coplanar.

questions.question: For an amino acid with two ionizable groups with \( pK_{a1} = 2.34 \) (carboxyl) and \( pK_{a2} = 9.60 \) (amino), its isoelectric point (pI) is:
questions.explanation: For a neutral amino acid without ionizable side chain: \( pI = \frac{pK_{a1} + pK_{a2}}{2} = \frac{2.34 + 9.60}{2} = \frac{11.94}{2} = 5.97 \).

questions.question: A polynucleotide chain has inherent chemical polarity and is synthesized in biological systems in which direction?
options: A) From the 5'-phosphate end to the 3'-hydroxyl end (5' -> 3')
B) From the 3'-hydroxyl end to the 5'-phosphate end (3' -> 5')
C) Bidirectionally from middle towards both ends simultaneously
D) Randomly along the nitrogenous bases
questions.explanation: DNA and RNA polymerases add incoming deoxynucleoside triphosphates exclusively to the free 3'-OH group of the growing strand, giving 5' -> 3' directionality.

questions.question: In competitive enzyme inhibition (e.g. malonate inhibiting succinate dehydrogenase), how are the kinetic parameters \( V_{\text{max}} \) and \( K_m \) affected?
options: A) \( K_m \) increases (apparent affinity decreases), while \( V_{\text{max}} \) remains unchanged
B) \( V_{\text{max}} \) decreases, while \( K_m \) remains unchanged
C) Both \( V_{\text{max}} \) and \( K_m \) decrease
D) Both \( V_{\text{max}} \) and \( K_m \) remain completely unchanged
questions.explanation: The competitive inhibitor binds reversibly to the active site. High substrate concentration overcomes the inhibitor, reaching normal \( V_{\text{max}} \), but requiring higher substrate concentration (increased apparent \( K_m \)).
